results.summary: This is a custom 8-bit RISC-V-inspired CPU with a hardware multiplier, 32 bytes of RAM, and custom branching instructions, implemented in Verilog for the IHP26a process. It uses a multi-cycle finite state machine to fetch, decode, and execute instructions, and includes a bootloader mode for loading programs via the input pins. To test, the user resets the chip, loads instructions and data into RAM using the address and data pins while mode select is low, then sets mode select high to run the program; the output pins continuously show the destination register value and the program counter. The design is notable for its compact 1x2 tile implementation and its custom branching instructions, and it requires only a clock source and logic analyzer or LEDs for verification.

This project implements a Turing machine in Turing's original mathematical construction, using external SPI ROM and RAM for the transition table and tape. It requires two 512Kbit SPI memory devices to be filled with data before execution, and the ROM can be emulated by the on-board RP2040. Testing is difficult because the SPI memories must be preloaded, and the design is not fully documented with step-by-step instructions. The design is notable for its faithful implementation of a theoretical computing model on a small tile.

This design implements a custom SPI module to interface with RHD2164 neural amplifier chips, selecting specific channels and transferring data to a microcontroller via SPI. It also includes a register bank accessible via SPI or scanchain/shift register. Testing can be done with an FPGA and emulators, or with a real RHD2164 chip in CMOS or LVDS mode using adapters. The design is notable for its biomedical application and flexible register access, but requires external hardware such as an FPGA or MCU and the neural amplifier chip.

This project is a scaled-down Spacewar game that outputs VGA graphics and audio, using a SNES controller Pmod for input. It adheres to old demoscene specifications and requires a TinyVGA Pmod and an audio Pmod to operate. The game starts directly after reset and is notable for its retro gaming implementation on a small tile. The documentation is partially complete, with some details on the gamepad and VGA connections but limited on the game logic.

This project is a 12-hour clock drawn with triangles using a race-the-beam triangle renderer, outputting to a VGA display via a TinyVGA Pmod. It uses a state machine that incrementally rasterizes triangles for the clock face, and the clock can be adjusted by asserting input pins 6 and 7. Silicon test reports indicate that the minutes and hours can be adjusted as documented. The design is notable for its efficient rendering algorithm and successful silicon verification.

This is a systolic binary neural network accelerator with 16 neurons, designed for AI/ML inference. It computes dot products between weights and input features, firing when the result exceeds a learned bias, and uses an 8-cycle systolic compute to reuse hardware and reduce silicon area. No external hardware is required beyond the Tiny Tapeout carrier; a Raspberry Pi or Arduino can load weights and run inference via the GPIO pins. The design is notable for its efficient systolic architecture and compact implementation.

This project tests two different implementations of C-gates (Muller C-element) and ring oscillators, with inputs A and B and outputs that change only when both inputs agree. The design includes latches and combinatorial logic, and the ring oscillator outputs are too fast to observe without an oscilloscope. The author manually verified the C-gate behavior by flipping inputs and observing outputs, but the ring oscillator test requires an oscilloscope and showed a sick waveform on one pin. The design is notable for its asynchronous circuit testing and the comparison of two C-gate implementations.

This project has essentially no documentation; the one-line description is 'I don't know yet' and the only pin is a generic input. It is likely a Wokwi-based experiment or template, but no functionality or testing details are provided. The summary is based on the minimal information available, and the design's purpose remains unclear.

This design implements a 32-bit iterative multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit with a 7x8-bit multiplier for AI/ML acceleration, targeting the LatchUp 2026 competition. It computes a 15-bit product every clock cycle and supports streaming weights and bias bytes from a host MCU via GPIO pins. No external hardware is required beyond the Tiny Tapeout carrier. The design is notable for its iterative architecture that balances area and throughput for tiny ML accelerators.
